claims.conditions: hatchery: Northeast River (Chesapeake Bay) strain, F1 broodstock at UW–Milwaukee, spawned 9 Oct 2018 (out of season); mean length on the day of hatch, measured in ImageJ (length type not stated); incubation at 16 °C constant, 12 °C rising 1–2 °C every 3–4 d, or that regime with a 16-h 10 °C shock
claims.note: 4.96–5.30 mm across treatments; the heat-shock treatment was not measured (too few larvae).

claims.claim: hatchery yellow perch ribbons yielded 19.9–49.6 % viable larvae
claims.quote: Steady 27.9 … Standard 30.8 … Cold Shock 49.6 … Heat Shock 19.9
claims.conditions: percent of eggs that were viable larvae (alive formed larvae plus ruptured, hatched eggs) at the end of incubation, by ImageJ counts of 3 ribbon samples per segment; 5 females' ribbons split across 4 temperature treatments; dead eggs 49–65 %, failed (eyed but dead) larvae 0.8–22.9 %

claims.claim: perch embryos tolerated a 16-hour cold shock to 10 °C better than a warm spell to 20 °C (49.6 against 19.9 % viable)
claims.location: p. 13 (PDF p. 22), Methods; p. 17 (PDF p. 26), Results
claims.quote: The cold shock treatment average (49.6%) was significantly higher than the heat shock
claims.conditions: shock on day 6 of incubation, 16 h at 20 °C (heat) or 10 °C (cold); p = 0.0325 (Tukey); the heat shock left three ribbon segments with no viable larvae

claims.claim: Guma'a's 97/(T − 4.9) × 1.2: yellow perch develop ~20 % slower than Eurasian perch (Linkenheld 2019)
claims.location: p. 17 (PDF p. 26), Results; p. 26 (PDF p. 35), Table 3 (incubation period)
claims.quote: The steady treatment larvae started hatching after 10 days post-fertilization (dpf)
claims.conditions: 16 °C constant ('steady'): hatch from 10 to 11 dpf, mean incubation 10.5 d (Table 3)
claims.note: Working: Guma'a's D50 = 97/(16 − 4.9) = 8.74 d; 10.5/8.74 = 1.20. The Linkenheld input is right; Guma'a's formula was not checked here (another entry). Caveat: Linkenheld writes that the steady and heat-shock larvae 'developed faster than normal for yellow perch' (p. 20, PDF p. 29) and the cold-shock larvae normally, so the ×1.2 drawn from the 16 °C treatment may understate the slowdown; the rising-temperature 'standard' treatment (12 °C up 1–2 °C every 3–4 d) took 12–13 d.

notes: Other values: ribbon sections of 72.5–90.9 g held 18,500–30,960 eggs (eggs = 280.2 × g + 607.6, r² 0.23); incubation 10.5 d at 16 °C, 12 d on the rising regime, 13 d after the cold shock; larval growth ~0.10–0.12 mm/d over 28 d, but larval survival was 0.3–2.3 % in the tanks, so the larval data are weak. Hatchery yields understate field viability (the paper says so already). The broodstock is a Chesapeake strain spawned in October, not a northern lake population.
